hypotheses.name: The IRGC, not Mojtaba, rules Iran (working model) — HELD 82%
hypotheses.d: HELD. The promised authenticated footage of Mojtaba meeting commanders still has not landed, so the falsifier remains un-run. The week was IRGC-forward — the Guard, not the foreign ministry, confirmed it ran the Oman channel and announced the revenue-sharing terms, and the Guard made the mine-strike claim — but that is DENIED as a raise under the shared-prediction rule: 'the Guard runs the maritime file' is predicted just as strongly by an ordinary reading in which the IRGC is a powerful institution under a functioning Supreme Leader, which is a much weaker claim than 'the IRGC rules Iran'. The 82% cap stands for exactly the reason it was set.

hypotheses.name: The Iran file is coalition-captured (the capture read, tracked as opinion)
hypotheses.d: The claim: on the Iran file, organized coalition pressure — donor networks, primary structure, allied commitments, defense-institutional momentum — outweighs the base's war fatigue, which is why a 'no more wars' White House struck anyway and now substitutes sanctions for settlement rather than sign a visible retreat before the midterms. Mechanisms named, plural: status clock vs electoral clock, sunk cost after declaring victory, lobbies as veto players that raise the price of defection (one interest group among several — any single-key version of this hypothesis is scored separately and currently rejected). Held at 70%: the strike itself, the 6-month grind, and 'not in a hurry' all fit; capped because the same facts also fit ordinary planning failure plus vanity. Falsifier: a signed de-escalation or negotiated Hormuz reopening BEFORE the midterms — the base's clock winning on the party's most captured file would kill the strong form outright.

hypotheses.name: Nobody's hurrying on Hormuz — 60% → 65% (RAISED)
hypotheses.d: Its first fact that BEATS a rival instead of merely fitting itself. On 30 Aug the US struck two IRGC rocket launchers on Larak after observing Guard personnel preparing to fire rockets carrying sea mines into the strait — two days after CENTCOM declared the lanes fully cleared, and while Muscat negotiates a minesweeping calendar. The 08-30 audit had installed a genuine rival — a physical clock, minesweeping simply takes time — and ruled this hypothesis must beat it. A physical clock runs down; this one is being rewound, by the exact actor the hypothesis named in advance. Capped at +5 on three counts kept in front: CENTCOM is the interested party and 'observed preparations' is unpublished intelligence used to justify a strike; Al Jazeera published a technical challenge on 31 Aug to whether Iran can even mine by rocket as claimed; and IRGC counter-coercion against a blockade that has redirected 83 vessels, disabled three and boarded two explains the same act without any rent motive. Not pre-event.

hypotheses.name: Détente as harvest cover — HELD 60%, tell sharpened
hypotheses.d: August continues the signature: 125 PLA aerial ADIZ incursions (the 2026 decline intact) against 152 non-warship PRC vessels in the first 21 days, ~60% coast guard, with the east-of-Taiwan patrols now a declared 'new normal'. Kinetic down, jurisdiction up. NOT moved — this is the same signal that bought +5 on 08-26, and re-marking on the continuation of its own evidence is the double-count the audit named. The important item is against my own test: if Beijing has DECLARED the patrols permanent, their persistence through the Sept 24 visit is close to uninformative. Re-specified now, in advance and stricter — the informative observation on 09-23→09-25 is a boarding, an inspection, or a first-time-area incursion. Mere presence no longer counts as confirmation.

hypotheses.name: Venezuela was a Hormuz hedge in a drug-war uniform
hypotheses.d: The clearest revealed-preference play on the board — and the reason it holds at 55 rather than higher. Sturdy mechanism first: US Gulf-Coast refineries are plumbed for heavy sour crude, Venezuela sits on the planet's largest heavy reserves, and moving that barrel north through the Caribbean to Texas and Louisiana structurally hedges the one risk that ran live all year — a Hormuz closure. The Aug 28-29 deal (a new operator taking control of ~65bn barrels, about a fifth of Venezuela's reserves) is exactly what this hypothesis predicts. So oil-as-motive is near-certain. What is NOT settled — and what caps this — is premeditation: was Southern Spear a counter-narcotics and regime-change campaign that harvested the oil after the fact, or an oil-security operation in a drug-war uniform from the start? The tell against design is the clock — the deal trailed Maduro's Jan 3 capture by eight months, which reads more like spoils than master plan. Falsifiers: token export volumes, Gulf-Coast heavy sourcing not actually swinging off the Middle East, or the fixed infrastructure (GEO-022) never appearing. One correction the excitement needs: a canal cannot bypass Hormuz — the hedge is source substitution plus Caribbean routing, not a waterway. Note it is DISTINCT from 'The Portfolio State' below, which is about the vehicle rather than the motive.

hypotheses.name: US drift hardened into leverage play — HELD 52%
hypotheses.d: Confirming but shared, therefore ambience: Treasury again held back on Chinese financial institutions, with mainstream reporting now naming the mechanism outright — designating them 'could create tensions before Xi's visit'. Bessent's promised weekly cadence hit banks but no Chinese one, and at the G20 he pushed severing Iran financial ties while China dissented. Both the leverage read and the ordinary 'Washington won't detonate its own summit' read predict all of it. The strongest weekly argument AGAINST, logged rather than absorbed: the US struck Iran on three consecutive nights and took Iranian fire onto three Arab host states. Deliberate slow-walking for leverage sits badly with sustained kinetic escalation that raises the cost of the thing being slow-walked — that counterweight is what holds the number at 52.

hypotheses.name: A pre-announcement leak into oil futures — 40% → 34% (biggest mover)
hypotheses.d: Its lead conditional has now gone unfired across three weeks containing the most violently market-moving Iran news since April — the 30 Aug Larak strike, three nights of exchanges, two struck VLCCs, Brent to ~$95 — with not one reported nine-figure pre-announcement episode. The file is confirmed as historical and bounded: DOJ is probing four trades totalling ~$2.6bn, all inside a five-week window that closed in April — Mar 23 (>$500m, ~15 min before Trump's delay post), Apr 7 ($960m before the ceasefire), Apr 17 ($760m, ~20 min before Iran said Hormuz was open), Apr 21 ($430m before the extension). CORRECTION BANKED AGAINST THIS ENTRY: the ledger's earlier '~$2.2bn cluster' for Mar 23 and its '~$7bn' aggregate are both withdrawn as over-wide constructions. The cut is made on the hypothesis's own written terms, not on a preferred reading — a conditional set at 60% has burned three of fourteen weeks in the best environment it will ever get and produced nothing. The cut is only −6 because of one genuinely new structural fact: investigators are running a SEPARATE probe into prediction-market activity on the same developments, and the same foreknowledge reaching two unrelated venues is hard to explain as one market-maker hedging client flow. Split now: deliberate leak 34 / mediator-side 20 / skilled opportunism 36 / coincidence 10. Still the only entry whose evidence is timestamped BEFORE the event.

hypotheses.name: NEW · The Portfolio State — coercion converted into sovereign equity, statute retrofitted
hypotheses.d: Strongest form: the US is converting military and sanctions leverage into permanent state equity in strategic supply chains, with the legal authority written to fit transactions rather than the reverse — Venezuela being the first hydrocarbon use of a template already run in chips and critical minerals. The rail predates the headline, which is the only thing licensing a design read at all: Senate NDAA FY2027 §1051 was marked up in MID-JUNE — ten weeks before the 29 Aug deal — creating a DoD Equity Investment Account, authorising OSC equity to $500m and capping any single position at 40% of the entity; the Venezuela stake is 35%, inside a cap that does not legally exist yet. Add DoD's own $400m/15% stake in MP Materials with 100% offtake (structurally identical to Venezuela's '20% of output at cost'), House Oversight already demanding an accounting of Venezuelan oil revenue on 23 Feb, and CFR's tally of 26 government equity deals worth ~$23.9bn. It opens at only 25% because the boring, incompetence and patronage readings are all strong: think tanks have been publicly naming and counting this pattern since 2025 (a policy, not a plot); the Pentagon's own spokesman flatly DENIES that OSC takes equity while WSJ reports it doing so, which is improvisation not design; and a 100-year concession over 65bn bbl routed to one politically connected operator with no published contract is better explained as spoils allocation. Above all the base rate is enormous — Anglo-Persian 1914, the RFC, GM/Chrysler 2009 — so the design premium must be small. NOT a conspiracy claim and must never be scored as one: it requires no secrecy at all, only anticipation, and the honest gap is that I cannot name the operator who executes the warrants. Key test: does the ENACTED NDAA widen §1051 beyond critical minerals to energy, or raise the cap, by 31 Dec (45%)? Scope enacted unchanged kills the design read.

hypotheses.name: Moscow shapes Tehran's maximalism — 25% → 22% (CUT, sixth session running)
hypotheses.d: The week finally produced Russia-Iran material and it is the wrong KIND. Moscow said publicly on 01 Sep that air defence is the main focus of military-technical cooperation with Iran, alongside a reported 500 Verba MANPADS and 2,500 missiles and continued fighter deliveries. That is the resupply leg — already priced at 7/10 under 'means'. It moves nothing: it is announced by TASS, an interested party publishing its own helpfulness and the structural opposite of a covert channel; the opportunism branch predicts arms sales to a client at war identically, so under the standing rule it is ambience; and after six sessions there is still ZERO documentary evidence Moscow has influenced Tehran's negotiating position, which is the actual claim. Arms transfers are not persuasion. Cut rather than held because a decay rule that bites only on its deadline is a cliff, not decay. Clock unchanged: 15% on 30 Sep absent documentary evidence, retire below 10%.

hypotheses.name: War pause was secretly packaged with the Beijing summit — on the retirement line
hypotheses.d: Nothing resolved this week, and one file addition cuts against it: the summit's Iran content is now openly reported as an explicit US ask — Chinese pressure on Tehran to reopen the strait — with Beijing expected to want Taiwan concessions in return. An openly negotiated Iran-for-Taiwan trade is this hypothesis's RIVAL, not its confirmation; the secret-package version needs the deal hidden, and the deal is being conducted in headlines. Retirement trigger unchanged; the test runs on schedule on 24 Sept.

brief.head: Saudi Arabia loses both of its oil export routes in one week
brief.h: The Ministry of Energy confirmed the 7 million barrel-a-day East-West Pipeline is shut as a precaution after drone strikes near Riyadh and Madinah, while Houthi forces took Perim island at the narrowest point of Bab al-Mandab - closing the Red Sea exit in the same week the Hormuz permit regime taxes the other one.
brief.t: The important thing here is not the fire, it is the geometry. Petroline exists for exactly one reason: it was laid across the peninsula so that Saudi crude could reach a Red Sea jetty at Yanbu WITHOUT passing Iran's guns at Hormuz. It is physical insurance against a chokepoint, bought after the last time a chokepoint was used as a weapon. This week both the insurance and the thing it insured against went offline together, and the kingdom's only remaining route out is the one Tehran now issues permits for. Follow the money and you find the second casualty nobody headlines: Yanbu is not just a jetty, it charges roughly 650,000 barrels a day of distillate-heavy refining aimed at Europe, and a crude line that is not pumping cannot feed a refinery. That is why we cut our diesel-crack question three points this morning rather than raising it - the shortage that matters is turning into a shortage of DIESEL, not of crude.
brief.context: Date the rail: this is a late chapter of the 1973-79 epoch in which oil was yoked to the dollar and the Gulf's surplus was recycled into Treasuries. Petroline was commissioned in 1981, during the Iran-Iraq tanker war, precisely as an anti-chokepoint asset, which makes today's closure the failure of a forty-five-year-old hedge rather than a new event. The desk that decides is not the royal court but the Ministry of Energy and Aramco's marketing arm, and their institutional objective is not retaliation - it is the reliability franchise, the reputation for never missing a cargo that lets Aramco price above spot. The base rate that governs is Abqaiq in September 2019: about 5.7 million barrels a day went offline, more than twice today's loss, and Aramco did NOT declare force majeure - it delivered from storage and substituted grades. That is why we hold that the confirmation of a shut valve and an actual failure to deliver are two very different objects, and it is also, embarrassingly, the base rate that made us misprice this exact question. The falsifier is a document, not a satellite image: if Aramco publishes an October Yanbu loading programme at normal volumes, this is an interruption; if the nomination window passes in silence, it is a production loss.

angles.effect: GAIN the strongest bargaining position of the war for free. Holding leverage over two chokepoints going into Monday's Salalah talks means more to sell and less reason to hurry - which is why our Hormuz-recovery question stayed at 10 rather than rising on the talks
PAYS twice - the routing cost now, and the deterrence cost of having announced in advance that it will not retaliate after being refused American strikes twice

angles.party: Asian refiners and European diesel buyers
angles.effect: PAY the freight. Barrels that cannot cross the peninsula must sail further or not at all, and the war-risk premium on Saudi-linked tonnage was already quoted several times the general Bab al-Mandab rate
GAIN a price they did not have to lobby for, which is also the reason a White House five weeks from a midterm is suddenly interested in refining capacity rather than crude

dec.kill: An Aramco October loading programme at normal Yanbu volumes turns this from a supply story back into a logistics story. So would a restart announcement on Petroline within two weeks.

consp.claim: Two claims are running side by side. The first is that the Iraq attribution is manufactured: the /pol/ Persia-Israel general lists the strikes on Saudi oil and electricity facilities under Ansar Allah's own operations, not Iraq's, and the circulating version says Riyadh and Washington are relabelling the launch site to build a legal case for hitting Iraq and, behind it, Iran. The second runs the other way and is louder in American commentary - that Washington is deliberately letting Saudi Arabia burn, refusing MBS's requests for strikes so that the kingdom is forced into whatever deal is being negotiated over its head.
consp.spread: The Persia-Israel general thread on /pol/, which is on its 2,115th edition and logs the pipeline strike as an Ansar Allah operation; aggregator posts headlined 'Huge Escalation' circulating the seizure plus the pipeline hit as one designed sequence; and mainstream-adjacent commentary amplifying that Trump refused the Saudi call for strikes.
consp.read: The first claim maps onto the classic false-attribution frame and has a checkable kernel: Baghdad's own investigation, not Riyadh's accusation, placed the launches in Maysan and dismissed a commander over it, which is a costly admission a government does not make to help a rival's cover story. The second is not a conspiracy so much as an unflattering description of a real policy - the refusals are confirmed and on the record - and the honest version is that leverage over an ally and indifference to an ally look identical from outside. What would separate them is whether Washington asks Riyadh for anything specific in the next month.

brief.head: BRICS opens in Delhi with a payment rail, not a currency
brief.h: Xi Jinping arrives in India for the first time in nearly seven years and Putin is already there as the 18th BRICS summit prepares to switch on BRICS Pay - a messaging layer stitching together Brazil's Pix, China's CIPS, Russia's SPFS and India's UPI - while New Delhi insists the point is cheaper trade rather than de-dollarisation.
brief.t: Read this as a fight over plumbing, not over flags. A reserve currency is a store of value; a payments rail is a way of sending MESSAGES about who owes whom. BRICS Pay is the second thing, and the second thing is what sanctions actually bite on - the 2022 lesson was not that the dollar is unpopular, it was that the messaging network that moves dollars can be switched off from Brussels and Washington. So the correct question is not 'does this end the dollar', which it does not and cannot, but 'does it make the next cutoff cheaper to survive'. Follow the money and the answer is modest but real: routing around correspondent banking saves fees and, more importantly, saves the deal from a compliance officer. Watch what India does with its hands rather than its mouth - Delhi is simultaneously building the rail and publicly refusing the anti-dollar label, because a US tariff threat is priced into every sentence its ministers say this week.
brief.context: Date the rail: this belongs to the epoch that opened in 1971, when the settlement unit stopped being gold and became a political object. Everything since - petrodollar recycling, SWIFT, CIPS, now this - is a fight over who administers the ledger. The desk that decides is not the leaders' podium but member central banks' payment departments and, in India's case, the Ministry of External Affairs weighing a tariff threat; Putnam's two-level game is the right frame, because Modi must look non-aligned abroad while not handing Washington a pretext at home. BASE RATE, and it is the whole discipline here: every BRICS summit since 2009 has produced the aspiration, and the count of declarations that named a binding, dated INSTRUMENT is approximately zero - which is exactly why our clock for this summit prices the naming of an instrument rather than the holding of the summit. Note the arithmetic that caps the story: intra-BRICS trade is a small fraction of world trade, the members run structural surpluses against each other in dollars, and no member's currency is convertible enough to be the unit. The falsifier is specific: a physical commodity cargo - oil, iron ore, fertiliser - settled end to end through this rail in a non-dollar unit, published with volumes, before the next summit.

angles.effect: GAINS the most and needs it most. A sanctioned economy pays a premium on every cross-border payment, and a rail that routes around correspondent banking converts a political cost into a technical one

GAINS optionality and PAYS in exposure. It gets a payments hedge and Modi gets the summit, but every step is measured against an explicit US tariff threat, which is why its ministers keep saying the word 'not' next to the word 'de-dollarisation'
GAINS reach for CIPS at someone else's summit - the rail's largest existing network becomes the de facto backbone without Beijing having to ask
PAYS almost nothing this year and something real over a decade. Each parallel rail lowers the marginal cost of the next cutoff being survived, which is a slow erosion of coercive power, not a run

dec.kill: A published, volume-disclosed commodity settlement through BRICS Pay in a non-dollar unit would move this from framing to substance. A summit declaration that mentions 'local currency trade' without naming an instrument, an operator and a date confirms the base rate.

consp.claim: That BRICS Pay is the operational start of the dollar's collapse, and in the harder version that it is a central-bank-digital-currency control grid being switched on under cover of a trade summit - with the corollary, heavily circulated in metals communities, that this is why physical silver and gold are being drained.
consp.spread: Crypto-and-macro aggregator sites running 'BRICS de-dollarisation agenda advances with global launch' headlines into X, and a 225-reply precious-metals general on /biz/ arguing a structural silver deficit alongside the summit, with an oil-price thread on the same board tying the two together.
consp.read: This maps onto the hedgehog frame Tetlock warns about - one big idea explaining everything - and it is doing real work for people selling metals. The checkable kernel is narrow and worth watching honestly: BRICS Pay is a genuine messaging and settlement layer with named national systems behind it, and the CBDC-linkage language is in India's own proposal, so the mechanism is not invented. What is invented is the timeline. It is downstream of the 2022 reserve freeze, which taught every non-aligned treasury that access is revocable; the emotional charge is real even where the arithmetic is not.

brief.head: North Korea fires missiles a day after allied drills wrap up
brief.h: Several short-range ballistic missiles flew from the Wonsan area toward the East Sea early Saturday, hours after the United States, South Korea and Japan finished the five-day Freedom Edge exercise; Seoul's presidential office convened an emergency security review and US Indo-Pacific Command said the launches posed no immediate threat.
brief.t: This is the cheapest legible sentence in international politics, and it is worth explaining why. A short-range ballistic missile fired into water costs Pyongyang almost nothing, breaks no threshold anyone will enforce, and produces a guaranteed response from three governments - an emergency meeting, a statement, a UN reference. It is a protest with a delivery receipt. The system underneath is a reciprocal-signalling loop that has run for two decades: allied exercise, launch, condemnation, next exercise. What makes this week different is not the missiles but the attention budget. Every American carrier group, every intelligence collection hour and every senior policymaker's calendar is currently pointed at the Gulf, and a regime whose entire strategy is extracting concessions for restraint reads a distracted patron as a discount. We are naming this on the board because our own ledger has NO Korean question at all, which is a coverage gap rather than a judgement that Korea is quiet.
brief.context: The rail here predates the current crisis by years: the 2019 Hanoi collapse ended the negotiated track, and Pyongyang's 2022 nuclear-use doctrine law codified what had been posture into statute, which is why later launches are legal-domestic events as much as military ones. The desk that decides is the General Staff's exercise-response cell, not the chairman's podium - launch timing tracks the allied exercise calendar with a lag measured in hours, which is a bureaucratic signature, not a strategic one. BASE RATE: short-range launches following major allied exercises are close to automatic, and the overwhelming majority are single events that produce no further escalation; the informative cases are the sequences and the category jumps. So the observable that matters is not this launch but the next fortnight - a second launch, an intermediate-range test overflying Japan, or a satellite attempt would each move this from ritual to message. Influence map: the principal is a regime that needs external threat to justify internal austerity; the market that prices it is South Korean sovereign risk and Japanese defence budgets, both of which barely moved.

brief.head: Colombia sends drones to spray coca after Washington cuts it off
brief.h: The de la Espriella government has authorised a seven-day pilot spraying roughly 1,000 hectares of Putumayo coca with glufosinate from low-altitude drones - the first aerial eradication since the courts stopped glyphosate in 2015 - weeks after the United States decertified Colombia as a counternarcotics partner and days after a visit by Secretary of State Rubio.
brief.t: Strip the drug-war language away and this is a clean case of a foreign government's pressure being transmitted through a domestic institution that may refuse it. Decertification is not a sanction; it is a formal American finding that a partner has failed on narcotics, and its bite is the aid, the trade preferences and the multilateral lending it puts in play. Bogota's answer is a spraying programme it has been legally forbidden to run for a decade. Notice how carefully it has been built to survive a courtroom rather than to kill coca: a different herbicide, a seven-day window, ten square kilometres, drones instead of crop-dusters, and a flight plan drawn around the indigenous and afro-descendant territory whose consultation rights are the exact hook the Constitutional Court used last time. That is the tell that everyone involved knows who the real decision-maker is. We opened a scored question on it this morning at 55 per cent - and pointedly not on whether Colombia sprays, which is already happening.
brief.context: The rail is judicial and it is older than this presidency. Aerial glyphosate spraying was suspended in 2015 after the IARC reclassified the chemical; Constitutional Court ruling T-236 of 2017 set prior-consultation and independent-evidence conditions on any resumption; and the Council of State blocked a restart in January 2022. Three interventions in a decade on one policy object is a high hazard rate, and it is the base rate our question is built on. The desk that decides is therefore not the presidency and not the US embassy but a Colombian court hearing a tutela petition - the constitutional injunction any affected citizen can file - which is why the programme's designers spent their effort on the flight plan rather than the chemistry. FRAMEWORK: Putnam's two-level game, where a leader negotiates abroad and at home simultaneously and can only deliver what the domestic table ratifies; American pressure is real, and it does not get a vote in Bogota's judiciary. What would change the read: the pilot completing with no petition filed, or conversely an injunction inside the first month, which would tell you the veto player is not merely alive but fast.

angles.effect: GAINS a visible answer to decertification at minimal operational cost. A 1,000-hectare pilot against a coca crop measured in hundreds of thousands of hectares is a political instrument, not an eradication strategy
GAINS compliance theatre it can point to, and PAYS if it now has to certify on the strength of a pilot - the standard it set was aggressive action, and it has been handed a test flight

PAY the health and livelihood risk. The herbicide is rated moderately dangerous by the WHO, and the consultation duty exists because the last programme's costs landed on people with no seat at either table
LARGELY UNAFFECTED at this scale, and historically advantaged by eradication that displaces cultivation rather than reducing it - the balloon effect is the most robust finding in this literature

dec.kill: If the programme scales past the pilot with no legal challenge, the veto-player read is wrong and the question goes to 25. An injunction inside the first month proves the opposite.

brief.head: UN gives Sudan's arms embargo one more month and no teeth
brief.h: The Security Council unanimously adopted resolution 2828, rolling the Darfur-only sanctions regime and its panel of experts forward by a single month to 9 October, while a US proposal to extend the embargo to the whole of Sudan stays deadlocked.
brief.t: The story is in the number of months. This regime is normally renewed for a year; renewing it for four weeks is the diplomatic equivalent of paying the minimum on a credit card, and it tells you the Council could not agree on the substance and did not want a lapse on the record. The substance is geography. The embargo has covered only Darfur since 2005, which in a war fought across the whole country by forces supplied across open borders is not a siege - it is a line drawn on the part of the map where the cameras were twenty years ago. Mulder's rule for reading any sanctions regime is to ask where the leakage path runs, and here the leakage path is the entire point: weapons and the gold that pays for them move through routes the resolution does not name. Extending it nationwide is the one change that would make the instrument match the war, which is precisely why it is stuck.
brief.context: Rail: resolution 1591 of 2005 built a Darfur-specific regime for a Darfur-specific crisis, and institutional inertia has kept the geography frozen through a war that has since consumed the country. The desk that decides is the Council penholder plus whichever permanent member is willing to spend a veto, and a one-month technical rollover is the standard bureaucratic device for parking a fight - historically it precedes either a watered-down renewal or a quiet lapse rather than a strengthened regime. BASE RATE, stated plainly: UN arms embargoes on active civil wars have a poor enforcement record, and the panel-of-experts mechanism is a reporting body without an interdiction capability, so what it produces is evidence, not prevention. Influence map: the principals are the two belligerent commands; the operators are gold refiners, freight forwarders and the re-export intermediaries the panel has repeatedly documented; the market that prices it is bullion in Gulf trading hubs; and the target is a civilian population with no seat anywhere in that chain. The falsifier for the pessimistic read is concrete: a nationwide embargo adopted by 9 October, with named designations attached, would show the Council can still match an instrument to a war.

angles.effect: GAIN a clean unanimous vote and avoid a lapse headline, at the price of another month in which the instrument does not match the war
GAINS the moral high ground of having proposed the nationwide extension, and PAYS nothing for it while the proposal is blocked - a costless position is not the same as a policy
GAIN four more weeks of a regime whose geography they already route around
PAY the entire bill. Famine conditions and mass displacement continue regardless of which month the mandate expires in

dec.kill: Adoption of a nationwide embargo with named designations before 9 October would falsify the read that this Council cannot move on Sudan.

consp.claim: That the embargo is deliberately kept narrow because a Gulf state - the United Arab Emirates - is arming one side and buying its gold, and that Western capitals will not act because they sell it weapons and bank its money. Circulating in a stronger form as an accusation of knowing complicity in genocide.
consp.spread: Boycott hashtags aimed at the UAE running across X, TikTok and Instagram, amplified by diaspora accounts and by advocacy organisations calling for an arms embargo on the UAE itself rather than on Sudan.
consp.read: The technique to notice is single-key causation - one actor made to carry a war with many suppliers - and it is worth naming because the underlying evidence is unusually strong for a circulating claim rather than weak. A UN panel of experts and Amnesty International have both published findings on re-exported weapons reaching Sudanese belligerents, and the gold trade routing through Gulf hubs is documented in the panel's own reports. So the checkable kernel is large: the panel's next report and any customs or re-export documentation are the falsifiable objects. What the single-key version loses is that the other side is also externally supplied, and that the Council's paralysis has more than one author.

watch: An Aramco October loading programme for Yanbu, at normal volumes or not at all. Now that the ministry has confirmed the valve is shut, this is the only document that separates a routing interruption from a production loss - and it outranks every statement either government makes.

Whether a second drone launch comes out of Iraqi territory after the Maysan dismissal. That one event settles whether Baghdad's sacked commander bought real control or only a delay, and it is the phrase "at this stage" that then has to cash.

The BRICS Delhi declaration, read for an INSTRUMENT rather than an aspiration - a named operator, a dated launch, a settlement volume. Every summit since 2009 has produced the aspiration; almost none has produced the instrument.

The FOMC statement on Wednesday, specifically the sentence about energy rather than the rate. The decision is already in the market; whether look-through language on oil survives is not, and that is what GEO-029 turns on.

Whether a tutela petition is filed against the Colombian spraying pilot, and how fast a court takes it. That is the veto-player test the new GEO-035 is built on, and the filing is public before the ruling is.
lesson: Today's lesson is the Sound Dues, and it explains why oil got CHEAPER on the day two chokepoints closed. From 1429 until 1857, Denmark charged every merchant ship passing through the Oresund - the narrow water between Denmark and Sweden - a toll simply for being allowed through. At its height the Sound Dues funded up to two-thirds of the Danish crown's revenue, and the crucial detail is that Denmark did not want to stop the ships. A blockade earns nothing. A toll earns forever, and it earns most when trade is heaviest, which gives the toll-keeper a direct financial interest in keeping the water open and merely expensive. The mechanism is worth a name: a chokepoint holder who builds an administration - a permit office, a fee schedule, an inspection regime - has revealed that they are pricing access, not denying it. Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority is a permit office with a fee schedule. What it predicts now is specific and testable: expect arrangements, corridors and toll structures rather than closure, expect the holder to fight hardest over who ADMINISTERS the passage rather than whether it opens, and expect prices to settle at a plateau above the old level rather than spiking to a shortage. That is exactly what our ledger says - a 76 per cent chance any Hormuz deal preserves Iranian transit machinery, against 10 per cent that traffic actually recovers. And the honest counter-case, because the Sound Dues also show how this ends: Denmark's toll was finally bought out in 1857 by a coalition of states that paid a lump sum rather than keep paying forever. Watch for someone offering Tehran the lump sum.

events.label: Perim (Bab el-Mandeb)
events.note: Houthi forces hold the island splitting the strait at its narrowest point, completing control of Yemen's western coast. The airstrip on it is the emplacement tripwire - a capture is not a closure.

events.label: Yanbu
events.note: Red Sea terminus of the shut East-West Pipeline, and the crude source for roughly 650,000 b/d of distillate-heavy refining. An October Aramco loading programme, or its absence, is the document that settles the story.

events.label: Abqaiq
events.note: Eastern-province origin of Petroline, which was laid in 1981 precisely so Saudi crude could reach the Red Sea without passing Hormuz. That forty-five-year-old hedge is currently offline.

events.label: Maysan, Iraq

quiz.q: Why does today's brief argue that shutting the East-West Pipeline is a DIESEL story as much as a crude story?
options: Because the pipeline carries refined diesel directly to European buyers
Because its terminus at Yanbu also supplies the crude charge for roughly 650,000 b/d of distillate-heavy refining, which cannot run without it
Because diesel is priced off pipeline tariffs rather than off crude
Because Saudi Arabia imports its diesel through the same pipeline in reverse
quiz.why: A refinery is a machine that needs a crude feed. Cutting the feed removes the products, not just the barrels - which is why the desk moved its diesel-crack question DOWN, away from the threshold, rather than up.

quiz.q: Oil prices FELL on the day a chokepoint was captured and a major bypass pipeline was shut. What does the brief say that pattern reveals?
options: That the reporting was exaggerated and little actually happened
That traders expect OPEC+ to release spare capacity immediately
That the market is pricing a higher cost of passage - a toll - rather than a physical shortage of oil
That oil markets no longer respond to Middle East events
quiz.why: A toll makes oil more expensive to move; a shortage makes it impossible to get. Prices that rise to a plateau and then fade on escalation are the signature of the first. In the staged template this is Stage A/B behaviour, not the Stage C shortage spike.

quiz.q: The new Colombia question asks whether a COURT will halt the spraying programme, not whether Colombia will spray. Why did the desk frame it that way?
options: Because courts are easier to forecast than governments
Because pricing an event that has effectively already happened is what produced today's worst-ever Brier score on the Saudi pipeline question
Because Colombian courts have never ruled on this issue before
Because US decertification legally requires judicial review in Colombia
quiz.why: Today's post-mortem is the lesson: GEO-032 scored a Brier of 0.314 because it priced something that was already physically true. A forecast has to sit on genuine uncertainty - here, the veto player - to be worth anything.

quiz.q: What is the analytical point of the Sound Dues, the toll Denmark charged ships passing the Oresund from 1429 to 1857?
options: That naval blockades reliably force political concessions
That narrow waters are impossible to defend without a large fleet
That a chokepoint holder who builds a permit office and a fee schedule is pricing access, not denying it - and therefore wants the water open but expensive
That international law has always guaranteed freedom of navigation
quiz.why: A blockade earns nothing; a toll earns forever, and earns most when trade is heaviest. That is why the desk expects corridors and fee structures out of the Hormuz talks rather than either closure or free transit - and why 76 per cent of the probability sits on any deal preserving Iranian administration of the passage.

quiz.q: A circulating claim says BRICS Pay is 'the operational start of the dollar's collapse'. Which observable would best test it?
options: The number of heads of state who attend the Delhi summit
Whether the summit declaration uses the phrase 'local currency trade'
Whether a physical commodity cargo is settled end to end through the rail in a non-dollar unit, with volumes published
Whether the US publicly criticises the initiative
quiz.why: Attendance, rhetoric and American irritation are all cheap and all present at every summit since 2009. A settled cargo with disclosed volumes is the one thing that cannot be produced by a communique - which is why it is the falsifier and the others are noise.

plumbing.epoch: E6, the 2008-2022 quantitative-easing rail in its unwind chapter, meeting E4, the 1973 security-for-barrels bargain - and today E4 was the one that moved. That bargain traded American security guarantees for dollar-priced oil, and its unstated assumption was that the guarantor would keep the sea lanes open and would show up when a client was attacked. Both halves of that assumption were tested in one day: a chokepoint changed hands, a fire burned over the only pipeline that routes around the other chokepoint, and the guarantor declined a treaty partner's direct request for strikes, offering intelligence and targeting data instead. The old rail: a security guarantee underwritten by a navy with forward basing. The new permit: the guarantee is now explicitly partial - freedom of navigation for the lane, but the land war behind it is the partner's problem - and that repricing is happening at the same moment the monetary half of the bargain is being asked to absorb a supply shock with a demand instrument.

sections.t: US diesel set an all-time record this week at $5.820 a gallon, and the crack spread — the refiner's fee for turning crude into something an engine can burn — printed an all-time $108 a barrel while Brent sat at an unremarkable $96. In the same week US missiles reportedly struck a tanker at Iran's Kharg Island anchorage, and Ukrainian drones held Russian refinery runs at 3.6m barrels a day, the lowest since May 2002.

Crude — the thing everyone photographs and embargoes — is behaving; refined product is not. A $108 crack means the market will pay more to convert a barrel than the barrel is worth: a fact about cokers and hydrotreaters, not about oil. Name the mechanism — the conversion bottleneck. The binding constraint is never the abundant input but the narrow step in the middle, which cannot be built on the timescale of a war or an election.

sections.h: Deep history I — Rockefeller never wanted the oil
sections.t: John D. Rockefeller owned almost no wells. He owned the refineries of Cleveland, and what he did with them in 1871 is the founding text of chokepoint economics. Tom Scott of the Pennsylvania Railroad chartered the South Improvement Company, and Rockefeller's terms inside it were breathtaking: the Erie, New York Central and Pennsylvania would pay the SIC a rebate of $1.06 on every barrel it shipped — and a drawback of $1.06 on every barrel shipped by refiners outside the club. He was paid when his rivals did business. The charter was repealed that April before a single transaction cleared, and Ida Tarbell's exposé later finished the job — but the insight outlived the scandal: crude is worthless until someone converts and moves it, and whoever owns the narrow step prices the wide one.

sections.h: Deep history II — the war decided at the still
sections.t: The largest test of this proposition was the Allied air war, fought inside the alliance before it was fought over Germany. Arthur Harris of RAF Bomber Command believed in punishment: burn the cities, break the will. Carl Spaatz and Arthur Tedder pushed what Harris dismissed as panacea targets — oil. Germany had almost no crude. It had Bergius hydrogenation, synthetic fuel pressed from coal at Leuna, Pölitz and Brüx, plants too enormous to hide. The oil plan began in May 1944. Leuna alone absorbed 22 raids, 6,552 bomber sorties and 18,328 tons of bombs across a year, behind Europe's heaviest flak concentration. It worked anyway. German synthetic output fell from a peak of 316,000 tons a month to 107,000 in June 1944 and 17,000 by September. Aviation gasoline — the specific fraction, not oil in general — went from 175,000 tons in April to 5,000 in September: 97% gone in five months. From May 1944 Germany consumed more than it produced every month, and the stockpile was gone in six.

sections.h: Deep history II — the fuel, not the factories
sections.t: The detail that makes it unforgettable: over the same period Albert Speer drove German tank and aircraft PRODUCTION to its wartime peak. The Reich ended 1944 with more airframes than it could fly and more panzers than it could move — the factories were fine and the fuel was not. The US Strategic Bombing Survey — written by people with every reason to praise bombing in general — judged the oil and transport campaigns decisive and the city campaign not. Japan lost the same way: the July 1941 freeze is remembered as an oil embargo, but the fatal shortage was 100-octane aviation gasoline, a conversion capability Japan could not build.

sections.h: Deep history III — how the West stopped building stills
sections.t: Now the slow part. The last greenfield major refinery built in the United States was Marathon's Garyville, Louisiana: built 1973-76, online 1977, still running at 596,000 barrels a day. Fifty years, no new plants — and the base is now shrinking: about 132 operable refineries in January 2025 against more than 300 in 1981, with roughly 1.235m b/d of distillation capacity removed in seven recent closures and conversions, over 6.5% of the total. All of it while shale made America the largest crude producer in history at 13.86m b/d. The country built the well and stopped building the still. The capacity emigrated rather than vanished — Jamnagar runs 1.24m b/d, Dangote opened at 650,000 and plans 1.4m, China kept building — so the toll moved east and south, to jurisdictions happy to buy discounted sanctioned crude and sell the product back to the people imposing the sanctions.

sections.h: The pattern — and where it breaks
sections.t: In all three cases the scarce thing is the transformation, and transformation capacity is inelastic over any politically relevant horizon: a new crude supplier takes a fortnight, a new hydrocracker takes five years and a billion dollars. Ukraine is now running the 1944 oil plan at a ten-thousandth of the cost, a drone flying 1,550km to Omsk doing what 6,552 B-17 sorties did to Leuna — Pape's denial thesis tested live. It breaks against me here: Germany had no crude and no neutral supplier, Russia has both, and a 24-year low in refining has not stopped Pokrovsk.

sections.h: The adjudication — Yergin and Blas vs Chris Miller
sections.t: THE ADJUDICATION — YERGIN AND BLAS versus CHRIS MILLER Yergin and Blas hold that energy chokepoints self-heal — inventories, bypass and rerouting absorb shocks forecast to be fatal — and they have been right about the barrel, Brent at $96 in a war that curtailed over 11m b/d. Chris Miller's Chip War argues the opposite for inputs that are not fungible: no reserve of fabs, no bypass for EUV, a decade to rebuild. The evidence splits them by step. Yergin and Blas won the crude argument; the crack is the market announcing the win does not survive one step downstream, because there is no strategic reserve of cokers — the US holds hundreds of millions of barrels of crude in the SPR and about a million barrels of distillate in the Northeast reserve, having stockpiled the input it cannot burn. Miller's case is still weaker in oil than in silicon: diesel is shippable in a way a fab's output is not, so refining heals in 12-24 months rather than 12-24 days.

OECD gasoline demand is in structural decline as EVs scale; diesel and jet demand are not, because trucks, ships, aircraft, mining and data-centre backup have no substitute. But a refinery makes every cut at once, so the economics that close Western refineries — falling gasoline — destroy the distillate capacity nobody meant to lose. A trap, not a cycle; confidence high. The bolder call, near 60%: by the mid-2030s the US is at once the world's largest crude exporter and a chronic net importer of middle distillates, and that buys a strategic PRODUCT reserve — legislated storage of diesel and jet, enacted after a winter shortage rather than before one. What keeps this honest is GEO-026: does the US diesel crack settle below $45 before 15 December 2026? It sits at 35%, so the house is 65% on regime rather than outage — and if the crack mean-reverts on the 2022 schedule, this is an elegant story about a spike, published as a miss.
